title: Mechanical Stimulation in Bone-on-Chip Platforms: A Systematic Review of Osteogenic Responses in Medical and Dental Applications
abstract: Abstract Bone healing, remodeling, and pathology are strongly regulated by mechanical stimulation. However, conventional two-dimensional (2D) in vitro culture systems fail to reproduce the complex mechanical and biological microenvironment of human bone, limiting their translational relevance. In recent years, bone-on-chip (BoC) platforms, as part of the broader organ-on-chip (OoC) technology, have emerged as advanced microfluidic systems that enable the study of bone biology under dynamic and highly controlled conditions that more closely mimic in vivo physiology. This systematic review aimed to gather the available in vitro evidence on mechanically stimulated BoC models, with a particular focus on osteogenic differentiation outcomes and the technical characteristics underlying these platforms. Following a comprehensive literature search and structured data extraction, biological parameters (cell types, culture conditions, scaffolds), chip design and fabrication strategies, mechanical loading modalities, and assessment assays were systematically analyzed. Across the included studies, fluid shear stress was the most frequently applied mechanical stimulus and was generally associated with enhanced osteogenic differentiation compared with static cultures, although substantial heterogeneity was observed in loading protocols and outcome measures. Overall, this review provides a consolidated technical and biological overview of mechanically stimulated BoC systems and highlights key methodological considerations for future platform development. By integrating microengineering approaches with bone and stem cell biology, BoC models hold significant potential for advancing bone tissue engineering, mechanobiology research, and translational applications, including dentistry-related bone regeneration and biomaterial testing.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Over the past few decades, organ-on-chip (OoC) models have rightfully gained a highlighted spot in medical and dental research field. The most recent EU directives turned the research interest away from animal testing by introducing the known as ‘3Rs rule’, promoting the Replacement, Reduction, and Refinement of laboratory animals’ usage [ 1 ]. Therefore, the development of more advanced  in vitro  models, and profoundly OoCs, was essential to bridge the gap to clinical studies and finetune the  in vitro -to- in vivo  extrapolation (IVIVE) process [ 2 ,  3 ]. OoCs are microfluidic devices that consist of microchambers/microwells on which the targeted organs are tissue-engineered (TEd), which can be dynamically cultured through microchannels [ 4 ]. Beyond reducing the use of laboratory animals and eliminating interspecies variability, these platforms markedly minimize experimental materials and culturing space, thereby increasing the data-to-materials ratio and offering a more sustainable high-throughput experimental model. These platforms are ideal for medical and dental material testing and provide promising biological assessment tools.

Among the various OoC platforms developed, bone-on-chip (BoC) systems have attracted particular research interest. Bone, apart from its structural, metabolic, and endocrine role, is continuously and dynamically remodeled [ 5 ]. Mechanical loading is vital for maintaining bone mass and structure, since it promotes osteoblast activity and reduces osteoclast bone resorption [ 6 ]. Osteocytes, found within the lacunocanalicular network act as mechanosensors and through a mechanotransduction process they convert mechanical strain and stress from fluid flow into biochemical signals that guide bone remodeling [ 7 ,  8 ]. Bone cells respond to various mechanical stimuli, such as compression, tension [ 9 ], fluid shear stress (FSS), hydrostatic pressure [ 10 ], and vibration [ 11 ]. These stimuli can change cell shape, organization of the cytoskeleton, and the expression of genes related to bone formation [ 12 ].

Historically, bone mechanobiology has been investigated primarily using conventional in vitro systems, such as static or dynamic cell culture models and stretch/compression devices, approaches that have clarified basic relationships between strain magnitude, load frequency, and bone adaptation [ 6 ] However, they are limited by interspecies differences and restricted control over local mechanical cues [ 13 ]. Regarding dentistry, these systems present difficulties in reproducing the complex interfaces of craniofacial tissues, such as the periodontal ligament (PDL)–bone or implant–bone junction.

To address these limitations, BoC platforms allow for analysis of osteogenic differentiation, extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition, and cell communication under mechanical loading and static and dynamic culturing conditions, therefore mimicking bone physiology closer than traditional static  in vitro  cultures [ 14 ]. Additionally, BoC models have also been used in various pathological models, including fracture healing, revascularization, and osteoporosis [ 15 ,  16 – 17 ].

In the context of dentistry, microfluidic systems and BoC platforms aim to mimic the alveolar bone and some oral and periodontal tissues, such as the PDL and oral mucosa. These tissues experience complex mechanical loads from mastication, parafunctional forces, removable dental prostheses, and dental biomaterial interfaces. This supports applications in periodontal disease treatment, bone regeneration, implantology, prosthodontics, and orthodontics. Alveolar-bone-on-a-chip and similar models that include oral cell types offer a more realistic view of oral mucosa, periodontal and peri-implant microenvironments than traditional  in vitro  systems. Moreover, periodontal-ligament-on-a-chip [ 18 ] and oral-mucosa-on-chip [ 19 ] systems now enable investigation of mechanobiology under controlled flow and loading, directly applying to orthodontic tooth movement, masticatory forces and alveolar bone remodeling under tension.

Despite this progress, studies on mechanical stimulation in BoC systems remain heterogeneous with respect to chip design, scaffold materials, cell type used and loading protocols, thus complicating direct comparison. Existing reviews do not comprehensively report how defined mechanical stimuli in these platforms influence osteogenic differentiation. Together, these gaps highlight the need for a focused synthesis of evidence on how different forms of BoCs and mechanical loading modulate osteogenic outcomes. Furthermore, only a subset of these BoC models were explicitly designed with dental application in mind, and few attempt to reproduce mechanical environments analogous to masticatory, prosthodontic or orthodontic forces typical of clinical practice [ 20 ].

The objective of this study was to systematically review the existing BoC incorporating mechanical stimulation models, in both translational medicine and dentistry fields. Specifically, this review focused on the recorded approaches on both physical and biological parts of the BoC, namely the methodologies followed for the chip device fabrication and the TEd analogues, thus providing a comprehensive and practical guide for the design and further development of future BoC models. Furthermore, the effects of external mechanical stimuli, including FSS, cyclic compression, tensile strain, vibration, and related modalities, on osteogenic differentiation in BoC and osteogenesis-on-chip platforms, were also evaluated and discussed, with particular emphasis on their impact on the osteogenic performance of TEd analogues. Finally, attention was given to dentistry-oriented BoC approaches and to the current limitations in reproducing clinically relevant masticatory, prosthodontic, and orthodontic loading conditions.

sections.heading: Methods and Materials
paragraphs: The protocol of this systematic review (SR) was registered at the “International Prospective Register of Systematic Review” (PROSPERO) with registration number CRD420251068806. The study was documented in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines [ 21 ].

sections.heading: Eligibility Criteria
paragraphs:
The eligibility criteria, based on the relevant Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, and Study type (PICOS) parameters are presented in Table  1 . In brief,  in vitro  preclinical studies that incorporated BoC technology to evaluate the osteogenic effect after mechanical stimuli were included. Any other models approaching bone pathology or exclusively evaluating other parameters, such as pharmaceutical components or material testing, were excluded from the study. Regarding used cell populations, only bone cells e.g. osteocytes, osteoblasts, osteoclasts, periosteal cells, or stem cells (SCs) differentiated to relevant cell types, were included.

No language or year limitations were applied. Any non-English studies were screened through their title and abstract and were translated using Google Translate. sections.heading: Selection and Data Collection Processes
paragraphs: The retrieved articles were collected in Rayyan platform to facilitate the screening process in two levels [ 22 ]. Initially, a manual deduplication procedure was followed. The selection process was conducted by two independent reviewers (AMT, CT), firstly by title and abstract screening and secondly, by full text screening according to the eligibility criteria. In case of discrepancies, they were resolved by consensus with senior authors (AB and FM).

For the data collection, an Excel sheet was created and filled. The sheet was checked before the data collection, in order to detect any omission or problem. The extraction process was performed independently by two reviewers (CT and AMT). Any discrepancies in the extracted information were resolved through discussion. In case of no consensus, a third reviewer (AB or FM) was consulted to adjudicate the final decision.

sections.heading: Data Items
paragraphs: The collected data items included bibliographic details, characteristics of the TE aspects (cell type details, culture conditions and scaffold), characteristics of the chip devices (design, fabrication method, and characterization), the methodology of mechanical stimuli, and the osteogenic assessment methods and results.

sections.heading: Study Risk of Bias Assessment
paragraphs: The QUIN Tool (Quality Assessment for In Vitro Studies) was used for the assessment of the risk of bias of the studies. The tool assesses 12 domains including details about the sample size, the sampling technique, the control group, clear explanation of the presented methodology, blinding of the assessors, randomization, statistical analysis and other. Each domain receives points whether it is documented by the authors or not (2 for adequately specified, 1 point if inadequately specified and 0 if not specified). If the domain is not applicable it is excluded from the calculation. The assessment was conducted by two reviewers independently (AMT and CT) and the final decision was made after comparison and if disagreement, the decision was made after the assessment of a third reviewer (AB). Finally, for each criterion, the percentage of studies receiving scores of 0, 1, or 2 was calculated by dividing the number of studies assigned to each score by the total number of included studies and multiplying by 100. The cumulative percentages were subsequently presented graphically.

sections.heading: Outcome Measures
paragraphs: The main outcome assessed was cell osteogenic differentiation. That could be estimated by mineral deposition through imaging or quantification such as ARS or ALP activity. Other stains could be used as Von Kossa and even X-ray imaging, for example through μCT. Gene expression could also be used as a differentiation estimation of osteogenic markers such as early transcription factors like Runt-related transcription factor 2 (RUNX2) or Osterix (OSX), or later markers like bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) or other. Also, ECM deposition could be an estimate of differentiation assessed via total collagen assay or gene expression. The timepoints preferred were 7, 14, 21, 28 days or more, however any other time point results were collected.
Secondary outcomes included cell viability, morphological changes, cytoskeletal alignment, proliferation were estimated.

sections.heading: Synthesis Methods
paragraphs: Due to high heterogeneity regarding cell types, stimulation, scaffolding, assays and chip designs, a meta-analysis was thought to be misleading and so was not conducted. A narrative synthesis was performed and findings were organized in tables. Study characteristics were presented in text and in tables along with relevant graphs. The main parts of the results included the cell types, culture conditions, scaffolds, chip manufacturing and design, and mechanical stimulation of the culture and assessment methodology of the osteogenic induction. Any material quantities were transformed in the same measurement unit for easier comparison between the studies. The results were preferably presented only qualitatively in order to depict the trend in each study between the groups compared.

sections.heading: Study Selection–Flow Chart
paragraphs: The PRISMA flow diagram illustrating the number of studies that were identified, removed, screened, excluded, and included, can be seen in Figure  1 . In brief, strings search on the selected databases retrieved 627 articles. After the deduplication process, titles and abstracts of 513 articles were screened. The collected articles ( n  = 66) were further assessed according to their full text. There were four main exclusion reasons: incorrect study type (e.g. reviews, conference abstracts,  in vivo / ex vivo  studies, or  in vitro  studies without BoC application), irrelevant cell type population (not bone cells or SCs, or the bone cells were combined with other no bone cell types to minimize the heterogeneity), non-eligible stimulation process (studies with no mechanical stimulation or with other externally applied stimuli), or not appropriate assessment method (no osteogenic differentiation/activity of the TE analogue). Finally, 24 studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the review. Fig. 1 PRISMA flow diagram with the number of studies per stage of identification

sections.heading: Risk of Bias
paragraphs: The results of the risk of bias assessment are depicted in Figure  2 . The overall risk of bias was high. The main domains which exhibited the greatest bias were the operator details, the randomization, the outcome assessor details and the blinding of the assessors. In all other domains, most of the studies had adequate reporting. Fig. 2 Risk of bias of the included studies as assessed by the QUIN tool. Green color indicates low, orange medium, and red high risk of bias

sections.heading: Cell Types
paragraphs: Illustrative graphs on the cell population details of the TEd analogues are depicted in Figure  3 . Among the included 24 studies, 14 studies utilized human origin cells with the main type being MSCs, being the predominant cell type, derived from sources, such as the bone marrow, adipose tissue, Wharton’s jelly, and PDL. Scheinpflug et al. isolated human osteoblasts from 4 different donors and Chiu et al. (2020) isolated periosteal cells from 7 donors to additionally assess inter-individual variability in gene expression patterns [ 27 ,  40 ]. One study used rabbit periosteal SCs. The remaining studies tested mouse cells, especially MC3T3-E1 pre-osteoblast cell line, MLO-Y4 osteocyte cell line and mBMSCs. sections.heading: Culturing Parameters
paragraphs: A great variety of culturing parameters was observed across cell types, some of which are illustrated in Figure  4 . The same cell type was cultured in different growth media depending on the study. MSCs were mostly cultured in alpha minimum essential medium (aMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), antibiotics and antimycotics. Alternatively, aMEM with 15% FBS [ 29 ], or Dulbecco’s MEM (DMEM) with 10% FBS, Roswell Park Memorial Institute (RPMI) 1640 medium with 10% FBS, or DMEM/F12 with 5 or 10% FBS were used particularly for ADSCs. Periosteal cells were cultured in RPMI 1640 with 10% FBS, while MLO-Y4 cells in aMEM with 2.5% FBS and 2.5% calf serum. The growth medium of MC3T3-E1 was in all cases aMEM with 10% FBS. Human osteoblastss were cultured in DMEM (of low glucose concentration) with 5% FBS, along with 5 mM L-alanyl-L-glutamine [ 40 ]. L-glutamine was added in other growth media as well, on different cell types [ 24 ,  25 ,  36 ,  38 ]. Macrophages, either the commercially available cell line RAW 264.7 or primary isolated cell populations were cultured in different media in each study. Fig. 4 Representative graphs on tissue engineered culture conditions extracted from the included studies, showing the percentages of  A  growth media,  B  serum type and concentrations, and  C  differentiation supplements

Cells were differentiated through the culturing medium in 15 of the 24 studies. Induced cell types included MC3T3-1, MSCs, and macrophages. Periosteal cells were not differentiated in any of the included studies. MLO-Y4 were induced only when co-cultured with macrophages. The main osteogenic differentiation supplements were dexamethasone, beta-glycerophosphate and ascorbic acid. Dexamethasone was most commonly applied at a concentration of 100 nM, while concentrations of 10 nM (two studies) and 5 nM (one study) were also reported. One study explicitly avoided the use of dexamethasone due to strong osteoinductive effect in order not to avoid masking the influence of mechanical stimulation. Beta-glycerophosphate was consistently used at a concentration of 10 mM. Ascorbic acid was most frequently applied at 50 μg/mL, although concentrations of 50 μmol/L, 50 mg/mL, 200, and 173 μM were also reported. In cultures involving macrophages, macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF) at 25 or 50 ng/mL, receptor activator of nuclear factor  κ B ligand (RANKL) at 10, 25 or 50 ng/mL, and 1a,25-Dihydroxyvitamin D3 at 10 or 20 nM were used as differentiation inducers. sections.heading: Scaffold
paragraphs: Summary graphs on the scaffolds used in the included studies are illustrated in Figure  5 . Of the 24 included studies, 15 did not utilize any scaffolds, while in 10 studies, only coating was applied, primarily collagen type I. Other coatings included fibronectin or polyethylene terephthalate (PET) [ 30 ,  41 ]. In two studies cells were cultured in spheroids and then positioned in the culture chamber [ 32 ,  37 ]. Finally, in three studies, cells were seeded directly on the deformable membrane, which was used for the application of mechanical stimulation. Fig. 5 Representative graphs illustrating the scaffolds used in the included studies, showing the percentages of  A  scaffold type,  B  coating type,  C  natural polymer type, and  D  other polymer types

The remaining studies employed bioceramics, natural polymers or synthetic materials as scaffolds. Atif et al. fabricated a biomimetic calcium-deficient HA via a cementitious reaction, combining tricalcium phosphate (TCP) with sodium phosphate dibasic (Na 2 HPO 4 ) solution to form a calcium phosphate cement (CPC) paste. Scaffold characterization included scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for morphological assessment, X-Ray diffraction (XRD) for crystalline phase identification, laser diffraction for particle size distribution, and a mechanical testing to evaluate compressive strength.

Regarding natural polymer scaffolds, three studies employed collagen hydrogels, composed of collagen type I; two followed a standard protocol for collagen gel formation, while the third a commercially available scaffold [ 40 ]. The first two were subjected to fluid stress for rheological characterization before application, and Babaliari et al. further characterized the scaffolds with SEM imaging [ 24 ]. In the study by Das et al., the scaffold consisted of gelatin combined with ultrasmall super paramagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (USPION) to enable magnetic forces application [ 28 ]. The nanoparticles were initially characterized using high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM), XRD, and superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) magnetometry. Subsequently, the scaffolds were characterized through SEM, Auger electron spectroscopy, nanoindentation, 3D optical surface profilometry and swelling ratio measurements. In the study of Lopes et al. a 3μL chitosan solution was deposited into the chip culture wells, neutralized and froze to form the scaffolds. Five human proteins (fibronectin, vitronectin, E-cadherin, collagen type I and amelogenin) were immobilized by mixing 1 μL of each protein with the chitosan scaffold, generating 31 different protein formulations representative of bone ECM, cell- cell contact junctions and enamel. Scaffold morphology was subsequently assessed using SEM.

Four studies employed synthetic polymers, two of which were fabricated using 3D printing techniques. Yamada et al. created a poly(L-lactide-co-trimethylene carbonate) scaffold through solvent-casting/salt-leaching technique [ 43 ]. Kim et al. fabricated porous bone scaffolds based on Gyroid and Schwarz diamond triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) architectures in several designs through computer-aided design (CAD) models to assess their effect on cell behavior, and to resemble bone physiology [ 33 ]. Fidelity between CAD designs and printed scaffolds was evaluated using micro-computed tomography (μCT) to assess pore size, porosity, and surface area, followed by compression testing. Zauchner et al. employed matrix metalloproteinases (MMP)- sensitive, microporous polyethylene glycol (PEG) hydrogels to investigated the role of matrix degradability in the osteogenic differentiation of human primary cells and ECM production [ 46 ]. Various PEG-based hydrogels were fabricated with or without peptides and crosslinkers to modulate scaffold properties. Pore size and other morphological characteristics were assessed by rhodamine labeling and confocal microscopy. Bahmaee et al. fabricated scaffolds through negative replica molding from PolyHIPE, a polymer made with 2-ethylhexyl acrylate (EHA) and isobornyl acrylate (IBOA) [ 25 ]. The mold was designed using CAD to generate a standard engraving over the scaffold to mimic bone morphology, which was further assessed by SEM. sections.heading: Chip
paragraphs: Negative molding was the primary fabrication approach used to produce chips, with polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) as the predominant fabrication material. Mold printing is primarily performed by soft lithography. Chip components- typically the microfluidic device, any incorporated scaffold, and a glass coverslip sealing the culture area- were bonded using plasma treatment or liquid PDMS. Considerable variability was observed in culture chamber parts and microfluidic channel dimensions. Whenever fluidic channels were present, pumps were used to drive growth medium through the system. These setups, along with a pressure meter accommodate the controlled pressure or flow rate of the respective circulating liquids, that provide nutrients to the TEd construct, while facilitating waste removal. Growth medium is provided through inlets and either it ends up in the waste reservoir or circulates through the culture system until removed and refilled in a couple of days. An alternative chip fabrication approach involved additive manufacturing, most commonly stereolithography, a high-precision 3D printing technique [ 25 ,  47 ]. Additional fabrication strategies included computer-controlled laser cutting machine of poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) components [ 39 ]. Glass slides, coverslips, and tubing were frequently incorporated to complete the assembly and enable controlled media perfusion.

When mechanical stimuli were applied through membranes on the TEd construct, the stimulus was usually applied below the cell culture area and the membranes were made from PDMS. For example, Chui and colleagues developed a 3x3 array culture chamber chip, with a deflectable PDMS membrane, so an open space below (air chamber) and above (culture chamber) the membrane were formed [ 26 ]. Pressurized air delivered by a pump into the air chamber induced membrane deflection and mechanical stimulation of the cultured cells. In a subsequent study, the same group modified the culture chamber dimensions and evaluated their effect on periosteal cell osteogenesis under mechanical loading [ 27 ]. Similarly, Yang et al. created a PDMS micro-system, where two parts surround a PDMS cell-seeded membrane, facilitating a single- or dual- chamber culture system [ 44 ].

In the study of Killinger et al., a multifunctional device was designed to operate as a miniature incubator, with its own CO2 and temperature systems, which provided the ability of monitoring through a regular inverted microscope [ 32 ]. The culture microfluidic device was positioned inside this construct and accommodated the uninterrupted perfused culture. The different parts were designed using a CAD software and were manufactured via a direct photolithography system or SU-8 resin-molds.

Scheinpflug et al. developed a microphysiological system capable of perfusion, environment-independent regulation of oxygen tension, and precise control and quantification of mechanical loading, supported by automated operation [ 40 ]. The microphysiological system was constructed by multiple 3D printed parts and could be parted in sections, specifically the application and quantification of the mechanical load unit, the culture unit, and the gas exchange unit. They used injection molding to create the cyclic olefin copolymer (COC), a biocompatible material which allowed the excitation of fluorescent emissions. The membrane was placed below the culture, and its deformation applied mechanical stimuli on cells, in an intermittent pattern, resembling interfragmentary movement during the fracture healing process.

Furthermore, Yamada et al. employed a custom-designed perfusion bioreactor incorporating peristaltic pumps and an integrated incubation system, including heating elements, electric fans, hydropressure sensors, a CO₂ sensor, and a temperature sensor [ 43 ]. Finally, two groups used commercially available chips [ 24 ,  37 ]. All extracted details on chips per included study are described in Table  6 .

sections.heading: Mechanical Stimulation
paragraphs: Summary graphs on the mechanical stimulation applied on the TEd constructs of the included studies are illustrated in Figure  6 . Most studies applied mechanical loading through microfluidic flow to exert mechanical forces on cells. These systems included a pump to regulate pressure and achieve the desired flow rates. The applied microfluidic flow rates varied across studies, while the respective flows were primarily of a steady and continuous rate. Air pump-connected deflectable membranes, magnets and ultrasound were utilized as alternative ways to apply mechanical stimuli on the TEd constructs. Fig. 6. Representative graphs illustrating the mechanical stimuli applied in the included studies, depicting the percentages of  A  mechanical stimuli type, and  B  microfluidic flow mode

Deflectable membranes were used in four studies. In the model developed by Chui et al. a multi-axial tensile strain was continuously applied to the cells for 1 or 3 days [ 27 ]. Growth medium was placed in the upper of the culture chambers. Similarly, Gao et al. developed a microfluidic device with a deflected membrane to induce oscillating tensile stress, which was carried out for 5 min in every 10 min interval and the total testing time lasted from 30 to 60 min [ 29 ]. The fluidic medium within the cell culture channel was static and replaced intermittently. In the study by Yang et al. 2021 a PDMS membrane with well-spread cells was stretched by its deformation generated by compressed air at 0.3 Hz for 2 days where 4 different pressure rates were applied (4, 5, 6, or 7 kPa), mimicking tensile strain [ 44 ].

In the study by Park et al. a distinct membrane-based loading approach was employed [ 39 ]. Pneumatic compression was inflicted via nitrogen gas to deflect a PDMS membrane periodically for 10 min every 12 h for 7 days. In this configuration, pressure was applied to the culture chambers and thus was induced directly on the cells and not on the membrane, as the previously presented studies. To minimize unintended shear stress, inlet and outlet channels connected to each chamber were temporarily blocked during loading. Cell culture medium was supplied using a passive hydrostatic pressure–driven method, avoiding shear stress during medium exchange. Similarly, in the study by Gao et al. the fluidic medium inside the culture chamber was static and replaced intermittently, so only the membrane deflection was estimated as a mechanical stimulation [ 29 ].

Several studies combined multiple mechanical stimuli. In the study by Scheinpflug et al. they used an elastomeric foil to cover the chamber below the culture chamber [ 40 ]. After the activation of the air pump, the foil moved towards the culture. Tissue constructs were mechanically loaded for a total of 8 h per day in 2 h loading periods, each followed by a 2 h break. Simultaneously, a constant flow rate of 0.5 mL/min was applied. Jing et al. applied ultrasound stimulation in addition to fluid shear stress (FSS) by positioning an ultrasonic probe beneath the chip, transmitting ultrasound directly to the microchannel [ 30 ]. In the study by Merife et al. a custom-made apparatus applied pulsed unidirectional fluid flow stimuli to address both fluid shear stimulation and cyclic compression on the matrix as mechanical loading [ 35 ].

Only in the study by Das et al. the mechanical stress was applied via magnets [ 28 ]. Ultrasmall super paramagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles were mixed with a gelatin scaffold. Two 0.05-T magnetic strength rare earth metal bar magnets (1 cm 2  area and 2 mm thickness) were attached to both sides of the reactor for magnetic actuation. Also, a flow rate of 1 mL/h was applied. sections.heading: Assessment Assays–Scope of the Studies
paragraphs: Summary graphs on the assessment assays of the included studies are illustrated in Figure  7 . The primary objective of the included studies was to assess the differentiation of the cells into osteo-cells. The most common assessment method was ARS and ALP staining, as well as the analysis of osteogenesis-related gene expression. Additional assessment techniques reported across the studies included calcium quantification, Von Kossa staining, and hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. For the osteoclastic phenotype the most commonly applied methodology was the telomeric repeat amplification protocol assay for collagen quantification. Overall, the most frequent investigation method was the quantification of gene expression, that allowed the assessment of shorter time points in order to show the trend towards an osteoblastic, osteocyte or osteoclast phenotype. Fig. 7 Representative graphs on the assessment methods used in the included studies, depicting the percentages of  A  experimental assays, and  B  differentiation gene expression

The evaluated time-points varied throughout the studies, from 1 to 35 days. To estimate the effectiveness of the mechanical stimulation, each study compared the relevant effect to the one of different culture conditions. Most commonly, mechanically stimulated tissue-engineered analogues were compared with static cultures including conventional non-stimulated 2D cultures in plates, wells, or dishes, as well as static cultures within microfluidic devices or on glass substrates. Additional comparisons included different flow or pressure conditions, mono-cultures versus co-cultures with other bone-related cell types, and different stimulation durations within the same experimental setup.

Several studies assessed cell differentiation through various non-direct assays, which indicatively reflect the induction trend of the cells, such as by evaluating cell morphology or polarization, and cell proliferation rate. Such parameters were evaluated using immunofluorescence imaging of the cytoskeleton, SEM imaging, live/dead assay staining, mitochondrial activity measurement or brightfield imaging in different time points. Finally, most studies incorporated vitality or proliferation assays to validate their setup before the differentiation potential assessment. Commonly reported viability assays included live/dead staining, Hoechst, and among the proliferation assays were CCK assay or Dehydrogenase assays like WST-1. sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: This systematic review (SR) summarized the available in vitro evidence using bone-on-chip (BoC) platforms to study the osteogenic effects of controlled mechanical stimulation. The first arm of the study examined how existing BoC models are biologically developed, in terms of cell populations, culture conditions, scaffolds, and extracellular matrix (ECM) selection. The physical aspects of BoCs were also assessed, namely chip design and manufacturing parameters, including chip layout, selected materials, and micro-architecture. The focus of these characteristics was their interaction with mechanically applied stimulation, which affects both the physical and biological components of BoC models. Finally, the osteogenic effects of applied mechanical stimuli, such as perfusion-driven fluid shear stress (FSS), cyclic compression or strain, and other device-enabled stimuli, were summarized and discussed. To this end, the review focused on common osteogenic readouts, including matrix mineralization assays and related gene expression, while also noting secondary outcomes such as viability, morphology, and other relevant indicators. The overall rationale of this SR was to serve as a systematic guide to existing BoC models and to inform future targeted research.

The overall pattern observed across the included studies was that mechanically dynamic conditions often produced stronger osteogenic signals than static cultures, particularly when multiple outcome measures were combined rather than relying on a single marker. This trend aligns with the established concept that bone biology is tightly regulated by mechanosensing, especially through osteocyte-driven networks that coordinate remodeling responses to physical cues [ 48 ,  49 ]. However, interpretation is not straightforward, as BoC studies differ widely in biological parameters, physical design, and stimulation protocols. This heterogeneity limited direct cross-study comparability and was the main reason why evidence was presented narratively rather than through meta-analysis, in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidance when quantitative pooling is not appropriate [ 21 ].

Regarding the biological aspects of BoC models, the SR systematically collected information on cell population combinations, species origin, and methods of cell establishment. In addition, details on culture and differentiation media were extracted, including media supplements and their concentrations, cell passage number, and culture duration. Scaffold and coating types, composition, and ECM analogues were also documented.

Most studies relied on mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) or osteoblast-like cells, with mouse-derived cells used in just over half of the models. In particular, MC3T3-E1 pre-osteoblasts predominated, while MLO-Y4 osteocytes and RAW264.7 macrophage cell lines were also frequently employed. This reflects broader trends in the BoC field, where MSCs and osteoblasts remain default choices for modeling osteogenesis due to their relative ease of isolation, expansion, and robust differentiation in vitro [ 16 ,  50 ]. From a mechanobiology perspective, however, the limited inclusion of osteocytes is noteworthy. Osteocytes are now recognized as the primary mechanosensors of bone remodeling, coordinating osteoblast and osteoclast activity in response to matrix strain and fluid shear [ 51 ,  52 ]. The fact that only a minority of studies incorporated osteocytes suggests that many current BoC platforms primarily model osteogenic differentiation rather than the full remodeling cycle. Moreover, among BoC models using human cells, MSCs were overwhelmingly preferred, and only the study by Vis et al. included a human bone cell type other than osteoblasts. Consequently, only restricted aspects of bone physiology are currently implemented, despite the well-established role of intercellular interactions in regulating osteogenesis and osteoclastogenesis [ 41 ].

Encouragingly, recent advances in bone remodeling in vitro are moving toward complex tri- and multi-culture systems that combine osteoblasts, osteoclasts, and osteocytes under controlled mechanical loading to better recapitulate tissue-level physiology [ 41 ]. In this context, the present findings highlight a gap between current biological understanding of bone remodeling and what is routinely implemented in BoC platforms.

Another biological feature emphasized by this SR was the prevalence of commercially available cell lines, which were used in 53.6% of the included studies instead of primary cell populations. This trend likely reflects their cost- and time-efficiency, ease of handling, extended passaging capacity, and reproducibility. In contrast, primary cells—despite higher maintenance demands and donor variability—more closely reflect native tissue physiology. As BoC technology advances, incorporating stable osteoblast–osteoclast–osteocyte co-cultures, ideally using human primary cells, will be an important step toward modeling long-term bone remodeling processes.

Substantial variability was observed in culture media, supplements, and differentiation protocols, reflecting a broader lack of standardization in MSC and bone-cell mechanobiology research, as also reported in previous reviews [ 53 ]. Many studies used the classical osteogenic cocktail of dexamethasone, ascorbic acid, and β-glycerophosphate [ 54 ]. While this approach reliably accelerates mineralization, it can also mask or confound the effects of mechanical stimulation. Dexamethasone, in particular, strongly promotes osteogenesis via upregulation of transcription factors such as RUNX2, even in the absence of mechanical cues [ 54 ]. Accordingly, the decision by Kim et al. to omit dexamethasone to preserve sensitivity to mechanical loading effects appears well justified [ 33 ]. Similarly, Bahmaee et al. compared osteogenic induction with and without dexamethasone. To mitigate this issue, most studies compared dynamic BoC cultures with static controls [ 25 ].

This review also underscored substantial divergence in scaffold strategies. Many models used no scaffold or relied solely on 2D coatings, most commonly collagen type I or fibronectin, effectively treating the chip as a flow-through culture system. While this simplifies fabrication and imaging [ 16 ,  50 ], bone tissue engineering literature consistently demonstrates that scaffold geometry, pore size, and stiffness significantly influence osteogenesis and angiogenesis, even prior to mechanical loading [ 55 ]. However, due to the greater technical difficulties of 3D cultures, that require versatile scaffolding or longer culture periods, these demands are fulfilled in a smaller number of studies, which is also depicted in the included studies [ 56 ]. This reduces the physiological relevance or the models, as the interactions between the neighboring cells and the effect of stress may differ from the ECM setting that is seen in bone [ 57 ]. To add on, it is known that cells respond differently in 2D than in 3D settings. Omitting 3D matrices may, therefore, underestimate how cells integrate biochemical and mechanical cues in vivo.

Identified scaffolds included calcium phosphate bioceramics, collagen- and PEG-based hydrogels, chitosan matrices, and 3D-printed constructs. Recent work on additively manufactured bioceramic and TPMS-based scaffolds demonstrates that curvature and pore interconnectivity guide osteogenesis and vascularization [ 58 ]. Several reviewed BoC models reflect this trend, such as PolyHIPE scaffolds supporting long-term osteogenesis under flow [ 25 ] [ 59 ]. Future studies should not only adopt advanced scaffolds more widely but also report their mechanical and structural properties in a standardized manner.

Across the included studies, most BoC devices were fabricated using polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), predominantly via negative molding and soft lithography, and operated using external tubing and pumps for perfusion control. PDMS enables rapid prototyping, good optical access for microscopy, and relatively simple integration of flexible membranes for strain or compression delivery. At the same time, the reviewed platforms adopted different layouts to accommodate distinct aspects of mechanical loading. Some platforms remained relatively minimal, embedding a single culture chamber with one culture medium flow, whereas others incorporated additional functions to better resemble physiological conditions, including miniaturized incubators designed to maintain stable culture environments. A clear example is the microphysiological system developed by Scheinpflug et al. (2023), which combined perfusion with controlled oxygen tension and quantified mechanical loading, directly addressing two parameters that are often poorly controlled in standard mechanostimulation experiments [ 40 ]. In contrast, other studies demonstrated that material selection itself may enhance osteogenesis; a similar concept was incorporated in the study by Killinger et al., which also employed transparent glass components allowing continuous microscopic observation of the culture [ 47 ]. Collectively, these findings indicate that BoC platforms constitute a broad umbrella concept rather than a single standardized technology. Consequently, the respective osteogenic effects are not directly comparable, and individual chip designs, material compositions, and manufacturing techniques should not be evaluated in parallel.

The most frequently applied mechanical cue in BoC studies was perfusion-induced fluid shear stress (FSS), as illustrated in Figure  8 . This likely reflects the natural compatibility between microfluidic device architecture and precise flow control, whereby shear forces can be systematically tuned through channel geometry and flow rate. Importantly, multiple studies suggest that shear does not operate under a simple “more exposure equals more response” rationale; instead, cellular outcomes depend on shear magnitude, the local microenvironment, and cell–material interactions that collectively modulate mechanotransduction. Xu et al. (2018) reported that osteoblast-like IDG-SW3 cells exhibited more pronounced morphological and organizational changes under higher shear (1.2 Pa) compared with lower shear (0.3 Pa), and that this response was further modulated by collagen coating density, highlighting that substrate conditioning and shear cannot be interpreted independently [ 60 ]. Chip designs that facilitate co-culture also reveal mechanically regulated cell–cell signaling under controlled transport conditions. Middleton et al. (2017) used a microfluidic co-culture system to examine osteocyte–osteoclast interactions, including migration and differentiation behaviors influenced by osteocyte-derived signaling under shear stress [ 36 ]. Overall, the dominant finding across studies was that mechanical stimulation increased differentiation toward osteoblast, osteoclast, and osteocyte phenotypes compared with static cultures. However, very low flow rates (< 2 μL/min) may inhibit osteoblastic differentiation while favoring cell proliferation. Fig. 8 Graphical illustration with a basic organ-on-chip model (on the left) and potential methodologies for external forces application on the system (on the right). The culture medium is provided to the tissue-engineered analogues through an external microfluidic device, which is controlled by a computer, while biological waste is removed through output tubing and collectors. External forces can be applied to the culture through microfluidic flow  a , membrane actuation  b , or sonication  c .

Although less common than flow-based approaches, membrane-based stretch and compression systems remain essential because they deliver mechanical inputs that may better resemble certain in vivo loading modes, such as tensile strain or compressive forces. These platforms also allow direct comparisons of biological effects under matched mechanical schemes. For example, Park et al. (2012) demonstrated that dynamic compression produced stronger osteogenic outcomes in BMSCs than in ADSCs under identical mechanical conditions, emphasizing that cell origin and baseline mechanosensitivity can strongly influence results and may partly explain heterogeneity across the literature [ 39 ]. Overall, these findings support the conclusion that OoC systems are practical tools for applying controlled mechanical cues; nevertheless, interpretation should be framed in terms of loading dose, mode, and biological context, rather than treating mechanical stimulation as a single comparable intervention.

Across the reviewed studies, the primary aim was typically to demonstrate that mechanical stimulation promotes osteogenic, osteocyte-like, or osteoclastic differentiation. This was most commonly assessed using mineralization assays (e.g., ARS, ALP-related assays), calcium quantification, and gene expression panels. The heavy reliance on gene expression appears rational, given its sensitivity at early time points and compatibility with the small sample volumes characteristic of microfluidic culture. However, this dominant assay strategy also limits interpretability, as expression-level shifts do not always translate into durable functional outcomes, including mature mineral deposition, structural remodeling capacity, or stable lineage commitment.

A key issue arising from these findings is the difficulty in isolating the specific contribution of mechanical signaling to improved osteogenesis. In perfused systems, enhanced delivery of oxygen and nutrients together with more efficient waste removal—hallmark features of dynamically cultured OoC platforms—can independently improve cell survival and metabolic activity. These effects alone may amplify osteogenic indicators such as gene expression, ALP activity, or mineral staining, even if the direct contribution of mechanical signaling is relatively modest. This issue is particularly relevant in three-dimensional cultures and spheroids, where static conditions can generate diffusion-limited zones, such as hypoxic cores, that impair viability and differentiation. For instance, Mishra et al. (2023) reported higher viability and enhanced osteogenic differentiation in PDLSC spheroids under flow compared with static conditions, while Killinger et al. (2023) similarly observed increased viability and mineralization in a dynamic microfluidic 3D culture device [ 32 ,  37 ].

Although studies involving additional pharmacological agents or biochemical stimulants were excluded from the present systematic review in order to isolate the effects of mechanical stimulation, several investigations remain worth discussing due to their relevance to dental and craniofacial research applications.

Specifically, the interaction between bone tissue and vascular structures was investigated by Chen et al 2025 [ 61 ]. In this study, a co-culture of HUVEC and hBMSCs was established to reproduce endothelial barrier morphology and evaluate its contribution to osteogenic mineralization. Although the study did not meet the inclusion criteria of the present review because of the simultaneous application of additional differentiation factors, the authors demonstrated that microfluidic flow (5 μL/min), combined with endothelial-mesenchymal cellular interactions, enhanced hBMSC differentiation and mineral deposition. Furthermore, lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulation was used to mimic the effects of  Porphyromonas gingivalis , one of the principal periodontal pathogens. Nevertheless, the independent contribution of mechanical flow could not be clearly distinguished from the effects of the biochemical stimuli and co-culture conditions.

Another clinically relevant disease model investigated the effects of bisphosphonate exposure combined with mechanically induced trauma [ 62 ] This topic is of particular importance in alveolar bone regions following tooth extraction or implant placement, where medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw may occur. Their platform successfully replicated aspects of inflammatory bone degeneration under mechanically stimulated conditions through a prototype strain-application device capable of delivering controlled mechanical strain to osteocyte cultures.

Finally, several bone-on-chip models have been developed to investigate cancer metastasis to bone; however, as this topic extends beyond the scope of the current review, readers are referred to previously published reviews for further information [ 63 ,  64 ].

Moreover, chip design influences the local magnitude of shear stress experienced by cells, such that identical applied flow rates can result in different mechanical stimuli at the cellular level. Many studies addressed this issue using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) or analytical modeling; nevertheless, reported shear stress values varied widely across studies, spanning μPa to kPa ranges. These observations support the benefits of dynamic culture but also highlight that perfusion provides multiple advantages, including nutrient transport, waste removal, and mechanical stimulation, whose individual contributions must be carefully disentangled. A deeper and more standardized characterization of the forces applied to OoC cultures would therefore better clarify the true mechanobiological effects relevant to bone physiology.

OoC models incorporating alveolar bone and oral cavity cells remain limited. Because bone in the orofacial area is characterized by distinct biomechanical features, such as the indirect forces generated during mastication, the biomechanical buffering effect of the periodontal ligament between the tooth/cementum and the alveolar bone, and the constant interaction with bacteria and inflammation, a unique microenvironment is created that remains difficult to replicate in vitro [ 65 ]. In addition to the oral cavity, the effects of malocclusion are also reflected in the temporomandibular joint, contributing to a wide spectrum of disorders that may impair the quality of life of patients [ 66 ].

The main experimental models investigating the effects of mechanical forces in orofacial bone are currently based on 2D cultures, animal models, simple  ex vivo  extracted teeth in substrates, or clinical studies in patients, without adequately reproducing the complex interactions between bone cells and their microenvironment [ 67 ,  68 ,  69 – 70 ]. On the other hand, OoC models developed so far have mostly investigated the interactions between different bacterial species and the effects of biomaterials on the oral mucosa. Furthermore, mucosa-on-a-chip, dentin-on-a-chip, and even tooth-on-a-chip systems have been established as pathophysiological models following exposure to pathogens (LPS) or dental biomaterials [ 20 ,  71 ,  72 ]. However, there remains a lack of OoC studies specifically investigating the role of masticatory or orthodontic forces in alveolar bone remodeling, highlighting an important translational gap in the field.

Regarding the results of the current systematic review, only the study of Mishra et al. used cells derived from the oral cavity [ 37 ]. PDLCs represent a heterogeneous cell population composed mainly of fibroblasts, but also mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), which under appropriate stimulation can differentiate toward an osteogenic lineage [ 73 ]. Since fluid flow inside bone is considered responsible for the activity of osteoblasts and osteocytes during tooth movement, along with the contribution of masticatory forces in bone remodeling, the findings of the present review could contribute to the future development of advanced 3D OoC models for the investigation of mechanobiological interactions during orthodontic treatment and mastication [ 74 ,  75 ]. Therefore, current OoC platforms still present an important translational gap regarding the accurate simulation of physiologically relevant masticatory and orthodontic loading conditions in alveolar bone.

Overall, the included studies were consistent in showing that dynamic conditions generally enhance osteogenic outcomes compared with static controls; however, variability in assays and controls often limits the ability to confidently explain why this occurs or to compare results across platforms. Although a fairly consistent trend suggests that mechanical stimulation in BoC platforms improves osteogenic outcomes, these findings should be interpreted with caution. First, the evidence varies substantially in terms of cell types, chip design, scaffold and ECM configuration, mechanical loading methods, dosing, outcome measures, and culture duration, preventing meaningful quantitative synthesis. Second, critical experimental details that reduce bias and enhance reproducibility, such as randomization, blinding, operator calibration, and transparent validation of applied mechanical forces, are often insufficiently reported, decreasing confidence in accuracy and generalizability, even when findings are consistent in direction. Third, many studies employ relatively short culture periods, limiting insight into late-stage mineralization and long-term remodeling processes. Physiological relevance is further constrained by the underrepresentation of osteocyte-focused models, despite their central role in mechanoregulated remodeling. In addition, the frequent co-investigation of mechanical and biochemical cues, particularly through the use of potent osteogenic supplements, can obscure whether observed effects are truly mechanical or primarily media-driven. Finally, although the field includes increasingly sophisticated platforms, such as systems combining quantified loading with microenvironmental control, many studies still lack comprehensive proof-of-concept validation [ 40 ]. As with all systematic reviews, relevant studies outside indexed databases may also have been missed. Collectively, these limitations indicate that while mechanical stimulation likely supports osteogenesis in BoC systems, improved standardization, rigorous reporting, consistent functional endpoints, and clearer experimental safeguards against bias are essential for establishing reliable dose–response relationships and enabling meaningful cross-study comparisons.
